facts.text: Tagline for this 1975 Mexican nunsploitation shocker: "From bride of Christ to slave of Satan!"
The title lives on: Salma Hayek's vampire-queen character Santanico Pandemonium in From Dusk Till Dawn (1996) is named after this film.
In Mexican theaters it premiered on June 26, 1975, under a different title: La sexorcista.
Frank's Movie Log notes the story opens with Sister María tending sheep near her rural convent, where she meets Satan, played by Enrique Rocha, who offers her an apple.
Shooting began in spring 1974 inside real convents in Tepoztlán, Morelos and Morelia, Michoacán, with interiors at Mexico City's Estudios Churubusco.
The film was inspired by British director Ken Russell's 1971 possessed-nuns shocker The Devils. Mondo Digital calls this one a variation on it, complete with a nun orgy.
Director Gilberto Martínez Solares directed more than 160 films, most from his own scripts, and is considered Mexican cinema's most important comedy director.
Surgeons of Horror's Saul Muerte describes the convent setting as stark and sun-bleached, an eerily calm backdrop for the film's escalating nudity, self-flagellation and blasphemy.
Before directing, Gilberto Martínez Solares started as a cinematographer, debuting on the 1935 film Rosario alongside his brother Raúl.
Director Gilberto Martínez Solares was a comedy specialist: he directed Germán Valdés "Tin-Tan" in the 1952 Snow White spoof before turning to Mexi-horror and wrestling monster movies.
A Google Arts & Culture exhibit says director Gilberto Martínez Solares once filmed as many as seven features in a single year: 1965.
Frank's Movie Log reports the mighty Mexican tourist board coproduced this nunsploitation film, which would explain all those real colonial convents on screen.
Enter Luzbel! Enrique Rocha, who plays the Devil, became one of Mexico's best-known telenovela villains, famed for his voice, after his 1965 breakout in La Mentira.
Enrique Rocha, Luzbel here, later voiced the panther Bagheera in the Spanish dub of Disney's 2016 The Jungle Book. He died November 7, 2021, aged 81.
Co-writer Adolfo Martínez Solares is the director's son. Mondo Macabro's Blu-ray includes his interview on making this film and the earlier House of Terror.
Its nudity in sacred spaces, flagellation and perverse rituals drew condemnation in heavily Catholic Mexico, according to Saul Muerte's retrospective at Surgeons of Horror.
Delia Magaña, playing the Mother Superior, was a veteran: the actress, singer and dancer appeared in Mexican films from 1930's Charros, gauchos y manolas to 1979.
Kurt Dahlke of DVD Talk wrote that the film "takes itself very seriously", focusing on the effects of chastity and blind religious obedience, despite its lesbian scenes and a rubber-knife stabbing.
Cultsploitation's Ryne Barber called the film "tactful in its methods": director Gilberto Martínez Solares favors eerie, surreal atmosphere over explicit gore and nudity.
Composer Gustavo César Carrión's brooding, noise-filled score is singled out for praise in Cultsploitation's Blu-ray review.
Mondo Digital's review says: "Rarely has a film's title been more appropriate than Satanico Pandemonium."
Saul Muerte of Surgeons of Horror gave it three stars, calling it "a memorable relic from a time when horror wasn't afraid to confront taboos with lurid abandon."
Mondo Digital suggests pairing this with Alucarda (1977), another Mexican convent-horror film, for maximum effect.
Surgeons of Horror lumps this Mexican shocker with other nunsploitation titles: School of the Holy Beast, The Nun and the Devil, and Flavia the Heretic.
Sister Maria's prayer, played by Cecilia Pezet: "If I worshipped you because I feared Hell, then let me burn in Hell." It is the film's best-known speech.
The film reached US home video on October 24, 1987, as Satanic Pandemonium: The Sexorcist, released on VHS by Eagle Video.
Wikipedia classes the film as an amalgam of witch-hunter horror and nunsploitation. Mexican cousin Alucarda (1977) tackles similar themes.
Co-writer Adolfo Martínez Solares says in a Mondo Macabro Blu-ray interview that the film's ending was reportedly left as an "open door" for the censors.
Eagle-eyed viewers report that in one stabbing scene, the blade of Sister Maria's fake knife visibly retracts into its handle.
